newsitem.title: USA: Lawmaker raises antitrust concerns about CBOT plan.
newsitem.headline: Lawmaker raises antitrust concerns about CBOT plan.

text.p: An Ohio congresswoman who sits on the House Appropriations committee said Thursday the Commodity Futures Trading Commission could find itself under legislative scrutiny if the agency approved a controversial change in soybean and corn futures contracts.

Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) urged the agency at a public hearing to reject the Chicago Board of Trade's proposed contract changes that would drop Toledo as a delivery point for corn and soybean futures.

The recommendation has become one of the most contentious issues ever to land before the CFTC, an agency that is fighting for its life amid pending legislation to strip it of most of its authority over U.S. futures exchanges.
More than 500 public comments -- most opposing the CBOT proposal -- were submitted to the agency this spring.

Kaptur, who has been a leading critic of the CBOT proposal to change delivery terms of the two giant contracts, said that she might take legislative action against the CFTC if it went along with the exchange.
She is a member of the House Appropriations committee, which is currently considering the agency's $60.1 million budget request for fiscal 1998, an increase of $5 million from the previous year.

"I would not rule that out. I don't think at this point it is necessary," Kaptur told reporters after appearing before the CFTC commissioners at a hearing that lasted more than four hours. The agency heard comments from the CBOT, state agriculture agencies in Michigan and Ohio, grain transporters, and a half-dozen other groups and companies.
"I feel so long as the process is fair, the decision that results will be fair," Kaptur said.

Kaptur also criticized what she described as the "arrogance" of the CBOT in resisting suggestions by Cargill Inc, Archer Daniels Midland, the American Soybean Association and scores of other companies and groups to modify the delivery proposal.

On Monday, Kaptur and 16 other lawmakers asked Attorney General Janet Reno to investigate the alleged anti-competitive impact of the CBOT recommendation to limit delivery points to the northern Illinois River. Reno has not yet responded to the letter, she said.

Kaptur told the five-member CFTC that she opposed the elimination of the port of Toledo because it would result in just four firms controlling 91 percent of the deliverable capacity on the northern Illinois River for corn and soybean contracts. Two of the firms -- ADM and Cargill -- have urged the CBOT to modify the delivery proposal to keep Toledo and rail options.

"Because of their diversified natures, these companies will be in the position of controlling delivery locations, barge freight and export facilities, raising grave concerns about the potential for price manipulation," Kaptur said.
